title: Where chase choruses came from
summary: The group discusses the origin of trading fours; Davenport ties it to jam sessions like prize fights, Wood to the Chicago crowd and older records.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Where did the idea of chase choruses come from? I don't know. You never heard anybody doing that?
And you don't remember when you first heard it?
The first time I heard that.
It started at those jam sessions.

Yeah, you know, like if a guy, like at one time, musicians used to be almost like prize fighters. If you find out a guy coming at the time, you're very good on a trick. Well, if you got a trick, like if I would find out Freddie Hubbard or somebody who knows, practice, for about two weeks. And when he comes in and plays, I would invite him somewhere to have a jam session. At that time, jam session was like a prize fighting match. Where everybody, well, this guy would try to, uh, to play this other way. I'd do a lot of them, but just play more music than me.
Well, some guys are boxers and some guys are sluggers. Yeah. And you can win by being a boxer, you can win by being a slugg, and the crowd likes sluggers.
So, like, after this guy takes a solo, takes his chorus, and this guy takes a chorus, then it's when you play chords. I play four, and you play four. Yeah.
Does that work on the record?
Oh, yeah. We live it on this one.
That's why I asked you. You're just for doing it, you know, but I wanted to know who was the first person. Well, I don't have to do that.
Yeah. I think, I think, I think you can actually find some of that on some old Tilly and Morton records. I'm not positive. I've never heard it on the old records.
That started, uh, doing the Bebop. I think it really started, uh, just before the Bebop era.
No, the Chicago crowd did it, because I get some records where Condon and Freeman and those guys.
Well, Bix and Tram used to do it, too.
